common_name: Trader Mulberry (Extreme-Cold-Hardy North Dakota Black-Fruited Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant own-root, cutting-propagated trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Trader is exceptionally cold-hardy and needs no winter protection even in northern plains climates where most mulberries suffer severe dieback or die outright.

directions: Trader is a US-patented (USPP28,932) black-fruited mulberry discovered in 2000 as the sole survivor of a grove of Morus alba seedlings that a German immigrant family named Trader planted near Oriska in Barnes County, North Dakota, around 1892; the original tree has since endured winter lows to -44 degrees F. Propagated on its own roots from cuttings rather than grafted, it bears abundant dark purple-to-black, nearly seedless fruit about 1 to 1.5 inches long with a flavor that starts tart at first color and sweetens within days, ripening sequentially over an extended midsummer-to-fall window rather than all at once. Mature trees develop an open, spherical crown and can eventually reach 30 feet or more, though most home plantings are kept smaller with routine pruning. Its combination of USDA zone 4 hardiness, self-fertility, and good resistance to spotted-wing drosophila makes it one of the very few reliably fruiting mulberries for northern gardeners where standard black mulberry (Morus nigra) cannot survive. As with other mulberries, ripe fruit stains heavily, so site it away from patios, decks, and walkways.
sources: Mayville State University plant breeding program (Kjelland/Walla, USPP28,932)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown plants in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Ho-O is grown as a foliage novelty rather than for its sparse fruit, and is typically stooled or coppiced hard each year to maximize new growth with the most exaggerated leaf texture.

directions: Ho-O is an ornamental white mulberry selection grown for its bizarre, tightly crinkled and crumpled foliage that bears almost no resemblance to typical mulberry leaves, giving it a strong conversation-piece texture in mixed borders and foliage-focused plantings. Left unpruned it can grow into a small tree to about 30 feet, but it is most commonly managed as a hard-pruned cutback shrub, cut nearly to the ground or to a low framework each late winter so it resprouts vigorously and tops out around 5 to 8 feet by season's end, since the most dramatically distorted, oversized leaves form on strong new growth. Fruiting is sparse and incidental; the cultivar is grown for foliage effect, not for a berry crop. Site in full sun to light shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and plan on an annual hard prune as routine maintenance rather than optional grooming.
